title: Brand New Easy Problem
statementMd:
A widely known among some people Belarusian sport programmer Lesha decided to make some money to buy a one square meter larger flat. To do this, he wants to make and carry out a Super Rated Match (SRM) on the site Torcoder.com. But there's a problem — a severe torcoder coordinator Ivan does not accept any Lesha's problem, calling each of them an offensive word "duped" (that is, duplicated). And one day they nearely quarrelled over yet another problem Ivan wouldn't accept.

You are invited to act as a fair judge and determine whether the problem is indeed brand new, or Ivan is right and the problem bears some resemblance to those used in the previous SRMs.

You are given the descriptions of Lesha's problem and each of Torcoder.com archive problems. The description of each problem is a sequence of words. Besides, it is guaranteed that Lesha's problem has no repeated words, while the description of an archive problem may contain any number of repeated words.

The "similarity" between Lesha's problem and some archive problem can be found as follows. Among all permutations of words in Lesha's problem we choose the one that occurs in the archive problem as a subsequence. If there are multiple such permutations, we choose the one with the smallest number of inversions. Then the "similarity" of a problem can be written as ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/e030ac55efb4d1b310573b6c32117d80ccefc0fd.png), where $*n*$ is the number of words in Lesha's problem and $*x*$ is the number of inversions in the chosen permutation. Note that the "similarity" $*p*$ is always a positive integer.

The problem is called brand new if there is not a single problem in Ivan's archive which contains a permutation of words from Lesha's problem as a subsequence.

Help the boys and determine whether the proposed problem is new, or specify the problem from the archive which resembles Lesha's problem the most, otherwise.

## Input

The first line contains a single integer $*n*$ ($1 ≤ *n* ≤ 4$) — the number of words in Lesha's problem. The second line contains $*n*$ space-separated words — the short description of the problem.

The third line contains a single integer $*m*$ ($1 ≤ *m* ≤ 10$) — the number of problems in the Torcoder.com archive. Next $*m*$ lines contain the descriptions of the problems as "$*k*$ $*s*_{1}$ $*s*_{2}$ $...$ $*s*_{*k*}$", where $*k*$ ($1 ≤ *k* ≤ 20$) is the number of words in the problem and $*s*_{*i*}$ is a word of the problem description.

All words from all problem descriptions contain no more than 10 lowercase English letters.

## Output

If Lesha's problem is brand new, print string "`Brand new problem!`" (without quotes).

Otherwise, on the first line print the index of the archive problem which resembles Lesha's problem most. If there are multiple such problems, print the one with the smallest index. On the second line print a string consisting of characters `[:`, character `|` repeated $*p*$ times, and characters `:]`, where $*p*$ is the "similarity" between this problem and Lesha's one. The archive problems are numbered starting from one in the order in which they are given in the input.

## Note

Let us remind you that the number of inversions is the number of pairs of words that follow in the permutation not in their original order. Thus, for example, if the original problem is "add two numbers", then permutation "numbers add two" contains two inversions — pairs of words "numbers" and "add", "numbers" and "two".

Sequence $*b*_{1},  *b*_{2},  ...,  *b*_{*k*}$ is a subsequence of sequence $*a*_{1}, *a*_{2},  ...,  *a*_{*n*}$ if there exists such a set of indices $1 ≤ *i*_{1} <  *i*_{2} < ...   < *i*_{*k*} ≤ *n*$ that $*a*_{*i*_{*j*}}  =  *b*_{*j*}$ (in other words, if sequence $*b*$ can be obtained from $*a*$ by deleting some of its elements).

In the first test case the first problem contains the "find the palindrome next" permutation as a subsequence, in which the number of inversions equals 1 (words "palindrome" and "next").

In the second test case there is no problem that contains a permutation of words from Lesha's problem as a subsequence.
statementZhMd:
一些人都知道的白俄罗斯著名竞赛程序员 Lesha 决定赚些钱，以便购买一套大一平方米的公寓。为此，他想在 Torcoder.com 网站上举办一场 Super Rated Match（SRM）。但问题在于，严厉的 Torcoder 协调员 Ivan 不接受 Lesha 出的任何题目，总是用一个冒犯性的词“duped”（即重复）来称呼它们。有一天，他们又因为 Ivan 不愿接受的另一道题目差点吵了起来。

现在请你扮演一名公正的裁判，判断这道题目是否确实是全新的，还是 Ivan 是对的，而这道题目与之前 SRM 中使用过的题目存在某种相似之处。

给定 Lesha 的题目描述，以及 Torcoder.com 题库中每道题目的描述。每道题目的描述都是一个单词序列。此外，保证 Lesha 的题目中没有重复单词，而题库中的题目描述可以包含任意数量的重复单词。

Lesha 的题目与某道题目之间的“相似度”计算如下：在 Lesha 题目中所有单词的排列中，选择一个作为子序列出现在题库题目中的排列。如果有多个这样的排列，则选择逆序对数量最少的那个。然后，题目的“相似度”可以表示为 ![image](https://espresso.codeforces.com/e030ac55efb4d1b310573b6c32117d80ccefc0fd.png)，其中 $*n*$ 是 Lesha 的题目中的单词数，$*x*$ 是所选排列中的逆序对数量。注意，“相似度” $*p*$ 始终是正整数。

如果 Ivan 的题库中不存在任何一道题目，其描述包含 Lesha 题目中所有单词的某个排列作为子序列，则称 Lesha 的题目是全新的。

请帮助他们判断给出的题目是否是全新的；否则，指出题库中与 Lesha 的题目最相似的题目。

## 输入格式

第一行包含一个整数 $*n*$（$1 ≤ *n* ≤ 4$），表示 Lesha 的题目中的单词数。第二行包含 $*n*$ 个以空格分隔的单词，即题目的简短描述。

第三行包含一个整数 $*m*$（$1 ≤ *m* ≤ 10$），表示 Torcoder.com 题库中的题目数。接下来的 $*m*$ 行每行包含一道题目的描述，格式为“$*k*$ $*s*_{1}$ $*s*_{2}$ ... $*s*_{*k*}$”，其中 $*k*$（$1 ≤ *k* ≤ 20$）是该题目的单词数，$*s*_{*i*}$ 是题目描述中的一个单词。

所有题目描述中的单词均只包含不超过 10 个小写英文字母。

## 输出格式

如果 Lesha 的题目是全新的，输出字符串 `Brand new problem!`（不含引号）。

否则，第一行输出与 Lesha 的题目最相似的题目在题库中的编号。如果有多道题目满足条件，输出编号最小的那道。第二行输出一个字符串，该字符串由字符 `[:`、重复 $*p*$ 次的字符 `|` 以及字符 `:]` 组成，其中 $*p*$ 是该题目与 Lesha 的题目之间的“相似度”。题库中的题目按照输入顺序从 1 开始编号。

## 说明

提醒一下，逆序对的数量是排列中顺序与原顺序不一致的单词对数量。例如，如果原题目是“add two numbers”，那么排列“numbers add two”包含两个逆序对——单词“numbers”与“add”组成的对，以及单词“numbers”与“two”组成的对。

如果序列 $*b*_{1},  *b*_{2},  ...,  *b*_{*k*}$ 中存在一组下标 $1 ≤ *i*_{1} <  *i*_{2} < ...   < *i*_{*k*} ≤ *n*$，使得 $*a*_{*i*_{*j*}}  =  *b*_{*j*}$，那么称序列 $*b*_{1},  *b*_{2},  ...,  *b*_{*k*}$ 是序列 $*a*_{1},  *a*_{2},  ...,  *a*_{*n*}$ 的子序列（换句话说，如果可以通过删除序列 $*a*$ 中的一些元素得到序列 $*b*$）。

在第一个测试用例中，第一道题目包含“find the palindrome next”这一排列作为子序列，其中逆序对数量为 1（单词“palindrome”和“next”组成的对）。

在第二个测试用例中，没有任何一道题目包含 Lesha 的题目中所有单词的某个排列作为子序列。
